vla_action_bins.Why do RT-1, RT-2 and OpenVLA turn each: Think about reusing the language model's softmax head and cross-entropy loss unchanged. Cover what a token per dimension buys (multimodal distributions, shared vocabulary) and what it costs per control step.
vla_action_bins.Why normalize actions with the 1st and 9: Consider what a single outlier does to a min/max range when the bin count is fixed. Cover bin resolution, clipping of the tails, and how dimensions that never move are handled.
vla_action_bins.With 256 bin edges from linspace(-1, 1,: Count edges versus intervals and recall that digitize returns an index in 1..n_bins. Walk through subtracting 1 and clipping to n_bins - 2 before indexing the centers.
vla_action_bins.Why does OpenVLA place action tokens at: Think about which BPE tokens are least used and what overwriting them costs. Write the forward map id = vocab_size - bin and its inverse, and say how ids outside that range are handled.
vla_action_bins.Compare the reconstruction error of Open: Compare where each scheme puts the decoded value inside a bin of width w. Cover the bias and the maximum absolute error of each, and what happens at the top of the range.
vla_action_bins.Per-dimension uniform bins versus a lear: Compare tokens per chunk, how correlation across time and dimensions is exploited, and what high-frequency control does to per-step binning. Mention decoding robustness to invalid tokens.
vla_action_bins.Discrete action tokens with cross-entrop: Weigh multimodality, ordinal structure between bins, precision, inference latency per action, and how much of the pretrained VLM head is reused.

fast_dct_action_tokens.What problem with per-dimension, per-tim: Think about token count (T times D per chunk) and how predictable the next token is at high control rates. Cover what that does to the per-token training signal and to dexterous, high-frequency tasks.
fast_dct_action_tokens.Why does applying a DCT along time make: Smooth signals concentrate energy in low frequencies. Explain what happens to high-frequency coefficients after scale and round, and why many zeros help the BPE stage that follows.
fast_dct_action_tokens.How do you build the orthonormal DCT-II: Describe each entry as a cosine of frequency times a half-shifted time index, and explain why row 0 needs a different scale. Then connect orthonormal rows to what C times C.T must equal.
fast_dct_action_tokens.Why flatten the coefficient matrix with: Consider what an autoregressive decoder predicts first and what it can stop early on. Cover where the informative coefficients and the long zero runs end up under each order.
fast_dct_action_tokens.Where does information get lost in the F: Name the two lossy steps: rounding and the clamp at min_token. Bound the rounding error per coefficient by 0.5/scale and use orthogonality to carry it to the actions.
fast_dct_action_tokens.How does the choice of scale trade recon: Relate scale to the rounding step size, to the range of integer values BPE must cover, and to how many high-frequency coefficients survive as non-zero.
fast_dct_action_tokens.FAST tokens with an autoregressive VLA v: Compare training speed and reuse of the language-model head against inference latency (many sequential tokens), precision limits from quantization, and decode failures on malformed token sequences.

act_temporal_ensemble.What problem does temporal ensembling so: Contrast open-loop chunk execution (jerky switches at chunk boundaries, slow reaction) with querying every step, where several overlapping chunks predict the same step and must be combined.
act_temporal_ensemble.In ACT's weights w_i = exp(-m * i), whic: Name the ordering of i (oldest to newest), then cover m > 0, m = 0 and m < 0 in terms of smoothness versus how fast new observations take effect. Mention ACT's default m.
act_temporal_ensemble.Derive the online update that adds one p: Start from avg_n = sum of w_i x_i over S_n, the sum of the first n weights. Multiply back by S_n, add the new weighted term, divide by S_(n+1). Say what state that needs per step.
act_temporal_ensemble.Why is a per-step count enough state to: Relate the count to which w and which prefix sums to use. Then count how many chunks can cover one step given each chunk spans K steps, and when a step leaves the buffer.
act_temporal_ensemble.The original ACT code finds populated pr: Explain why a zero-filled buffer needs a populated test, what happens to a real action with a zero entry, and how explicit counts replace the sentinel value.
act_temporal_ensemble.Temporal ensembling versus executing eac: Compare policy calls per step, how quickly a new observation affects the executed action, boundary jumps, and the risk of averaging two different modes.
act_temporal_ensemble.Temporal ensembling versus real-time chu: Consider inference latency longer than a control step: ensembling needs a fresh chunk every step, while async execution and RTC keep acting during inference and keep chunk continuity by guidance instead of averaging.

pi0_flow_matching_chunk.In pi0's flow-matching action head, whic: Name openpi's choice (noise at t = 1, integrate down to 0) and contrast it with the paper and SD3-style noise at 0. Cover the interpolation, the sign of the target, the sign of dt, and why a checkpoint is tied to one convention.
pi0_flow_matching_chunk.Why does pi0 generate a whole chunk of f: Think about control rate, error compounding and multimodality. Cover continuous outputs without binning error, one denoising pass producing H actions for 50 Hz control, and how a generative head represents several valid ways to act.
pi0_flow_matching_chunk.Walk through one Euler step of pi0 sampl: Start from the noise end and say which way time moves and how far per step. Then use the linear interpolation to relate x_t, t, v and the clean chunk, and ask what a constant velocity means for Euler error.
pi0_flow_matching_chunk.How does a committed action prefix enter: Cover the training side (prefix positions get the clean-end time, so x_t equals the actions there) and the sampling side (write the prefix into x). Explain what the network sees if you skip the clamp before, and what the output holds if you skip it after.
Sketch the Beta(1.5, 1) density (rising toward 1) and map it to the noise-at-one convention. Discuss why noisy times are the hard part of the field, and what a sample at exactly t = 0 would teach the network.
pi0_flow_matching_chunk.Few Euler steps versus many at robot con: Weigh latency per chunk against integration error on a curved learned field. Mention pi0's 10 steps, the cost of each step (a pass through the action expert with a cached prefix), and when Heun, rectified flow or consistency distillation pay off.
pi0_flow_matching_chunk.Flow-matching action chunks versus discr: Compare pi0 with pi0-FAST: token cross-entropy trains faster and reuses the LM head, but decoding is autoregressive; flow matching needs several denoising passes yet outputs continuous chunks in parallel. Discuss precision and multimodality on each side.

rtc_prefix_guidance.What problem does Real-Time Chunking sol: Cover the latency gap: d control steps pass during inference, so the first d actions of the new chunk are already executed from the old one. Name the jerk at a naive chunk switch and frame the fix as inpainting.
rtc_prefix_guidance.Why are the first inference_delay steps: Committed steps cannot change, so they must match exactly. Then discuss continuity: a soft exponential ramp over the overlap keeps the new chunk close to the old plan without pinning steps the robot could still improve.
rtc_prefix_guidance.Walk through one guided denoising step:: Name the three pieces: x1 = x - time * v predicts the clean chunk, the error is (prev - x1) * W, and the VJP pulls that error back through x1 to x_t. Mention the sign of the update in the Euler step.
rtc_prefix_guidance.Why must x_t require grad before the vel: Autograd only records ops on tensors that require grad when they run. Explain what the graph from x to v looks like in each order, and what J^T err reduces to if v is a constant.
rtc_prefix_guidance.How does the guidance weight behave as t: Write the weight in terms of tau = 1 - time and evaluate each factor at both ends. Say which undefined or infinite values appear, which value each end should take, and why a cap on the weight matters with few sampling steps.
rtc_prefix_guidance.RTC guidance versus hard inpainting that: Compare continuity at the boundary, extra compute (a backward pass per step) and what happens when the prefix is off-distribution for the model, for guidance versus overwriting the prefix after each step.
rtc_prefix_guidance.RTC versus ACT-style temporal ensembling: Contrast averaging overlapping chunks at execution time with conditioning generation on the committed prefix. Cover inference frequency, latency hiding, and mode averaging for multimodal action distributions.

symlog_twohot.What problem does symlog solve for Dream: Think about returns that span many orders of magnitude across tasks, and about gradients of a squared error on raw values. Cover what symlog does near zero and far from it, negative values, and why fixed normalizers or running statistics are fragile.
symlog_twohot.How does a two-hot encoding turn a conti: Consider which two bins bracket the target and how the mass is split between them. Cover the weights as ratios of distances, what the expected bin position equals afterwards, and in which space the target is compared with the bins.
symlog_twohot.Walk through building the two-hot target: Walk through the comparisons that give the two bracketing indices, the clipping to the valid range, and the case where both indices land on the same bin. Name where a zero gap would appear and how upstream avoids it.
symlog_twohot.Why does DreamerV3 compute the expected: Think about a zero-initialized output layer giving a uniform softmax, and float32 rounding in a left-to-right sum. Cover how pairing mirrored bins cancels exactly, and why a tiny bias matters for bootstrapped value targets.
symlog_twohot.What is the gradient of the two-hot cros: Start from the softmax cross-entropy derivative. Cover what the target contributes, why gradients should not flow through the target construction into y, and how the gradient scale compares with an MSE on large values.
symlog_twohot.Interpolating between bins in symlog spa: Compare where each scheme puts the linear interpolation, what each decodes exactly for a single target, and what each learns when targets are noisy. Bring in the gap between symexp of an average and an average of raw values.
symlog_twohot.A two-hot categorical value head versus: Compare gradient magnitude as targets grow, the ability to represent multimodal returns, the hard range of the bins, and the cost of a K-way output layer and softmax per prediction.

rssm_kl_balance.Why does DreamerV3 split the KL between: Think about the two ways the KL can shrink: the prior can move, or the posterior can drop information. Cover which network each term trains and why the weights favor one side.
rssm_kl_balance.What are free bits, and why are they app: Cover what the floor does to the value and the gradient below it, and what it protects against. Then compare a per-group floor: how the total budget changes and whether a few groups can still carry the information.
rssm_kl_balance.Where exactly do the stop-gradients go i: Name which logits are detached in each term and why the values stay equal. For the check, describe taking gradients of each term separately with respect to both inputs and what each must look like.
rssm_kl_balance.Why is unimix applied to the probabiliti: Compare what mixing does in each space to the smallest probability a class can have. Cover how that floor limits the log-ratio, and what goes wrong when the posterior is confident about a class the prior rules out.
rssm_kl_balance.What happens to the gradient of an entry: Cover the value and gradient of a clamped entry, then think about which losses drive the latent once the KL is silent. Consider what happens to representations that carry more information than the dynamics can predict.
rssm_kl_balance.Discrete categorical latents with straig: Weigh gradient bias against variance, how each handles multimodal futures, KL stability, and what unimix or a variance floor does in each case. Mention which DreamerV2 and V3 chose and why.
rssm_kl_balance.The original DreamerV3 uses beta_dyn 1.0: Think about the ratio of the two weights rather than their size. Cover how fast the prior catches up with the posterior, how much the posterior is regularized, and how this interacts with the free-bits floor.

jepa_block_masks_and_loss.Why does a JEPA predict the target encod: Think about what a pixel loss forces the model to spend capacity on. Cover unpredictable detail such as texture and noise, what an abstract target lets the encoder discard, and how that shows up in frozen-feature probing.
jepa_block_masks_and_loss.Both the prediction and its target come: Name the trivial solution first, then the pieces that keep training away from it: the stop-gradient on the target branch, the slow EMA target, the predictor in between, and the normalization of the targets.
jepa_block_masks_and_loss.V-JEPA 2 masks the union of several bloc: Consider how much video repeats from one frame to the next. Cover what the model could copy if only some frames of a region were hidden, and why short-range and long-range block sizes are mixed.
jepa_block_masks_and_loss.Each sample's context and target index l: Start from how the index lists become one batched tensor for the encoder. Then look at the flat index order: which time steps and rows sit at the end of each list, and so which tokens get dropped.
jepa_block_masks_and_loss.Why are the target features layer-normal: Separate the two choices. For the norm, think about the scale and offset of the regression targets. For the stop-gradient, think about what the loss could reward if it could also move the targets.
jepa_block_masks_and_loss.L1 versus L2 regression for the latent l: Compare how the gradient's size depends on the error under each exponent. Cover a few badly predicted tokens dominating the batch, behaviour near zero error, and why the loss divides by the exponent.
jepa_block_masks_and_loss.A constant EMA momentum such as 0.99925: Relate the momentum to an effective averaging window in steps. Cover early training, when the online encoder changes fast, and late training, when a frozen-looking target helps, plus what changes when the run length changes.

st_transformer_attention.What does a spatial layer attend over in: Name the token group each layer sees (one frame, one patch position across frames). Compare the size of the attention matrices against full attention over T * N tokens and say which term dominates.
st_transformer_attention.Why is Genie's temporal attention causal: Think about what the model generates frame by frame and what it may know at frame t. Cover one-pass next-frame training as in a decoder-only LM, and why patches of the same frame can see each other.
st_transformer_attention.Write the boolean masks that make ordina: Fix a flattening order first, then recover frame and patch from a token index. Describe each mask as a condition on the frame and patch of query and key, and say whether the diagonal is included.
st_transformer_attention.How do you reshape a (B, T, N, D) tensor: Cover which axis must end up as the sequence axis and which axes fold into the batch. Explain why a transpose is needed before the reshape and what a reshape without it silently mixes.
st_transformer_attention.After one spatial layer and one temporal: Trace the information path through both layers and the residuals: which frames and which patch positions are reachable. Then redo the trace with the order swapped and compare.
st_transformer_attention.Factorized space-time attention versus f: Weigh direct pairwise interactions across frame and patch against the depth needed to recover them. Bring in token counts for real video clips and where memory, not compute, is the limit.
st_transformer_attention.Separate weights for the spatial and tem: Consider whether spatial and temporal relations want the same query-key geometry. Cover parameter count, what the paper and open-genie do, and how positional embeddings interact with the choice.

world_model_cem_step.How does the cross-entropy method turn a: Walk through one planning iteration: what is sampled, what the world model predicts, how each sample gets a score, and which statistics the refit carries forward. Then say which action is executed and when the planner replans.
world_model_cem_step.Why does V-JEPA 2-AC minimise an energy: Contrast what each world model predicts: an embedding compared with a goal image versus rewards plus a terminal value estimate. Cover what the goal supplies in each case and why that fixes the direction of the elite selection.
world_model_cem_step.Why does TD-MPC subtract the maximum eli: Think about the range of floating-point exp and the size of predicted returns. Cover what the shift does to every weight, why it cancels in the normalisation, and what the largest weight becomes after the shift.
world_model_cem_step.What goes wrong with an unbiased std whe: Consider the divisor of an unbiased estimate with one sample and what that value does to the next sampling round. Cover options such as rejecting it, a floor on the std, or a biased estimate, and what each does to exploration.
world_model_cem_step.How do the momentum values on the mean a: Treat each momentum as an exponential moving average over iterations. Cover how the std momentum controls how fast the search narrows, why mean and std may need different values, and what momentum 0 and 1 each reduce to.
world_model_cem_step.Uniform elite averaging versus softmax w: Compare how each update reacts to one sample whose score is inflated by model error, and how fast each concentrates on the best region. Mention the role of the temperature and how it moves between the two behaviours.
world_model_cem_step.CEM planning at test time versus a learn: Compare the cost per action (many rollouts per step versus one forward pass), how each handles a new goal at test time, and how each is affected by world-model errors that an optimiser can exploit.
